title: A rebase stopped mid-flight. Continue, skip, or abort?
summary: Rebase replays commits one at a time, so it can stop several times in one run. Learn what state you are actually in, and which of the three exits you want.
mental_model: A rebase is a loop: check out the new base, then apply each commit in turn. When one fails to apply, the loop pauses with that commit half-applied and a conflicted index. You are on a detached HEAD, mid-loop — not on your branch.
danger: Running `git commit` instead of `git rebase --continue` during a pause creates an extra commit and leaves the rebase running. Always use --continue.

commit.message: Raise the ceiling further after bench testing

steps.title: See what will collide
steps.why: Both branches edited MAX_RPM. Rebasing replays your three commits one by one onto main's version, so the collision happens on the first commit — and only that one.

steps.title: Start the rebase and get stopped
steps.why: Git applies 'Raise the RPM ceiling' onto main's 3000 and cannot decide. Read the output carefully: it names the commit it was applying, which is the thing people skip past.
steps.expect: CONFLICT, and status says 'interactive rebase in progress' with the current step.

steps.title: Understand where you are standing
steps.why: You are on a detached HEAD partway through the replay. Your branch ref still points at the old, unrebased tip — nothing has been lost, which is why abort is always available.
steps.expect: HEAD, not feature/limits — and a done file listing the steps completed so far.

steps.title: Bail out completely, to prove you can
steps.why: `--abort` unwinds everything: the branch, the index, the working tree. Knowing this exit exists makes the whole operation far less frightening.
steps.expect: Exactly the state you started in.

verify.label: abort put you back on your branch

steps.title: Start again and resolve it properly
steps.why: 3000 from main is higher than your 2500 and was bench tested, so main wins here. Stage the resolution — but do not commit.
steps.expect: Nothing conflicted, changes staged, rebase still in progress.

steps.title: Continue — and get stopped a second time
steps.why: Two things happen at once here. Your first commit now contributes nothing (you took main's value), so git drops it silently as empty. Then it moves to commit 2 of 3 and hits a *different* conflict on the same file. A rebase stops once per problem commit, not once per rebase — the single biggest surprise for people used to merges.
steps.expect: Rebasing (2/3), a fresh CONFLICT, and the floor commit now half-applied.

steps.title: Resolve the second conflict and finish
steps.why: This commit raises the floor to 600, which is still what you want — main's ceiling and your floor are not in competition. Resolve to keep both, stage, and continue. Note you never run `git commit`: `--continue` does it, preserving the original message.
steps.expect: Rebase complete, branch reattached, two commits on top of main.

verify.label: the rebase finished and reattached your branch

steps.title: Read the result, and note your undo
steps.why: Three commits went in, two came out: the redundant one was dropped as empty. `ORIG_HEAD` still holds the pre-rebase tip, so `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` puts everything back even now that the rebase has finished.

verify.label: two commits replayed, the emptied one dropped

steps.title: The third exit: --skip
steps.why: `--skip` throws away the commit currently being applied and moves on. Git effectively did that for you when the patch became empty. Reach for it deliberately only when a commit is genuinely redundant — never to make a conflict you do not understand go away.
steps.expect: Nothing to do here — this step is the note, not an action.

verify.label: you are back on your branch, rebase finished
the emptied commit was dropped, the other two replayed
verify.hint: resolve each stop with git add then git rebase --continue

verify.label: main's ceiling and your floor both survived
verify.hint: resolve in favour of the bench-tested value, keep your own change

verify.label: no rebase left in progress and a clean tree
main was never modified — a rebase moves your branch, not the base

pitfalls: During a pause you are on a detached HEAD. `git commit` there makes a stray commit and confuses the rebase — always `git rebase --continue`.
A rebase can stop once per commit. Finishing one conflict does not mean you are done; read the output each time.
`--skip` throws the whole commit away, not just the conflicted part. Use it only for genuinely redundant commits.
`git rebase --abort` before it finishes, `git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD` after. Both are complete undos.
Turn on `rerere.enabled` and repeated rebases of the same branch stop re-asking the same questions.
cheatsheet: tells you which step of the rebase you are on
undo a rebase that already finished
